name: Kamalanatha Perumal Temple, Thiruvanvandoor
deity: Vishnu as Kamalanathan, known locally as Pambanaiyappan, with the Goddess Kamalavalli Nachiyar
period: A Divya Desam of Malai Nadu (Kerala), sung by Nammalvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Ancient Malai Nadu shrine; administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board
summary: At Thiruvanvandoor near Chengannur, Vishnu is worshipped as Kamalanathan, called Pambanaiyappan locally — a Malai Nadu Divya Desam sung by Nammalvar and attributed by tradition to the Pandava Nakula.

sections.history: Thiruvanvandoor, in Alappuzha district near Chengannur, is home to a Divya Desam sung by Nammalvar, whose reference to the shrine is placed around 800 CE and is the earliest on record for the temple. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvar saints in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and belongs to Malai Nadu, the Kerala country. The presiding Lord is worshipped as Kamalanathan, and locally as Pambanaiyappan, a name linked with the river Pamba; the Goddess is Kamalavalli Nachiyar. A form of Krishna as Gosala Krishna is also worshipped here. Today the Travancore Devaswom Board administers the temple. Among the five Pandava-linked Vishnu temples of the Chengannur country, tradition assigns Thiruvanvandoor to Nakula.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Kerala shrine of the Chengannur country, and its sanctum houses Vishnu as Kamalanathan, with the Goddess Kamalavalli Nachiyar honoured in her own right. A shrine to Gosala Krishna, Krishna among the cows, adds a second centre of devotion within the precinct. The names of the vimana and the tank are not firmly recorded, so none is given here; the visitor will find a quiet village temple whose character lies in its worship and its long attested devotion.
sections.legends: Tradition attributes the temple to Nakula, the fourth of the Pandava brothers. It is one of five Vishnu shrines around Chengannur each said to be tied to a brother: Thrichittatt to Yudhishthira, Puliyur to Bhima, Aranmula to Arjuna, Thiruvanvandoor to Nakula and Thrikodithanam to Sahadeva. Together they are remembered as the Pancha Pandava temples. The local name Pambanaiyappan ties the Lord to the Pamba river that waters the country around.
sections.festivals: The principal event is a ten-day annual festival in the Malayalam month of Kumbham (February–March), which opens with the flag hoisting and ends with the arattu, the ritual bathing of the deity. During these days the temple offers annadanam, the sharing of free meals, and presents Kathakali performances. Vaikunta Ekadashi is observed too. Dates follow the temple’s own calendar, so confirm locally.
sections.experience: A quiet village Divya Desam, best visited with the other Chengannur-area Pandava temples. Take darshan of Kamalanathan and then the Gosala Krishna shrine, and enjoy the unhurried pace of the precinct. In the festival days of Kumbham the temple fills with devotees, the flag, the meals and the Kathakali giving a very different, joyous mood.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions, usually with a midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvanvandoor is a village in Alappuzha district a few kilometres from Chengannur, which is the nearest railway station; autorickshaws, taxis and local buses serve the short road journey. Thiruvananthapuram and Kochi are the usual airport gateways.
